### Node.js Version

title: Linking and Navigating
description: Learn how the built-in navigation optimizations work, including prefetching, prerendering, and client-side navigation, and how to optimize navigation for dynamic routes and slow networks.
related:
  links:
    - app/api-reference/components/link
    - app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading
    - app/guides/prefetching
---

In Next.js, routes are rendered on the server by default. This often means the client has to wait for a server response before a new route can be shown. Next.js comes with built-in [prefetching](#prefetching), [streaming](#streaming), and [client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions) ensuring navigation stays fast and responsive.

This guide explains how navigation works in Next.js and how you can optimize it for [dynamic routes](#dynamic-routes-without-loadingtsx) and [slow networks](#slow-networks).

## How navigation works

To understand how navigation works in Next.js, it helps to be familiar with the following concepts:

- [Server Rendering](#server-rendering)
- [Prefetching](#prefetching)

Instead of reloading the page, it updates the content dynamically by: 00155| 00156| - Keeping any shared layouts and UI. 00157| - Replacing the current page with the prefetched loading state or a new page if available. 00158| 00159| Client-side transitions are what makes a server-rendered apps _feel_ like client-rendered apps. And when paired with [prefetching](#prefetching) and [streaming](#streaming), it enables fast transitions, even for dynamic routes. 00160| 00161| Next.js also handles [scrolling to the top of the page](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#scroll) during client-side transitions. If content scrolls behind a sticky or fixed header after navigation, you can fix this with CSS [`scroll-padding-top`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#scroll-offset-with-sticky-headers). 00162| 00163| ## What can make transitions slow? 00164| 00165| These Next.js optimizations make navigation fast and responsive. However, under certain conditions, transitions can still _feel_ slow. Here are some common causes and how to improve the user experience: 00166| 00167| ### Dynamic routes without `loading.tsx` 00168| 00169| When navigating to a dynamic route, the client must wait for the server response before showing the result. This can give the users the impression that the app is not responding. 00170| 00171| We recommend adding `loading.tsx` to dynamic routes to enable partial prefetching, trigger immediate navigation, and display a loading UI while the route renders. 00172| 00173| ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/loading.tsx" switcher 00174| export default function Loading() { 00175| return 00176| } 00177| ``` 00178| 00179| ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/loading.js" switcher 00180| export default function Loading() { 00181| return 00182| } 00183| ``` 00184| 00185| > **Good to know**: In development mode, you can use the Next.js Devtools to identify if the route is static or dynamic. See [`devIndicators`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/devIndicators) for more information. 00186| 00187| ### Dynamic segments without `generateStaticParams` 00188| 00189| If a [dynamic segment](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes) could be prerendered but isn't because it's missing [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params), the route will fallback to dynamic rendering at request time. 00190| 00191| Ensure the route is statically generated at build time by adding `generateStaticParams`: 00192| 00193| ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" switcher 00194| export async function generateStaticParams() { 00195| const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json()) 00196| 00197| return posts.map((post) => ({ 00198| slug: post.slug, 00199| })) 00200| } 00201| 00202| export default async function Page({ 00203| params, 00204| }: { 00205| params: Promise<{ slug: string }> 00206| }) { 00207| const { slug } = await params 00208| // ... 00209| } 00210| ``` 00211| 00212| ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.js" switcher 00213| export async function generateStaticParams() { 00214| const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json()) 00215| 00216| return posts.map((post) => ({ 00217| slug: post.slug, 00218| })) 00219| } 00220| 00221| export default async function Page({ params }) { 00222| const { slug } = await params 00223| // ... 00224| } 00225| ``` 00226| 00227| ### Slow networks 00228| 00229| On slow or unstable networks, prefetching may not finish before the user clicks a link. This can affect both static and dynamic routes. In these cases, the `loading.js` fallback may not appear immediately because it hasn't been prefetched yet. 00230| 00231| To improve perceived performance, you can use the [`useLinkStatus` hook](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status) to show immediate feedback while the transition is in progress. 00232| 00233| ```tsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.tsx" switcher 00234| 'use client' 00235| 00236| import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link' 00237| 00238| export default function LoadingIndicator() { 00239| const { pending } = useLinkStatus() 00240| return ( 00241| 00242| ) 00243| } 00244| ``` 00245| 00246| ```jsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.js" switcher 00247| 'use client' 00248| 00249| import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link' 00250| 00251| export default function LoadingIndicator() { 00252| const { pending } = useLinkStatus() 00253| return ( 00254| 00255| ) 00256| } 00257| ``` 00258| 00259| You can "debounce" the hint by adding an initial animation delay (e.g. 100ms) and starting as invisible (e.g. `opacity: 0`). This means the loading indicator will only be shown if the navigation takes longer than the specified delay. See the [`useLinkStatus` reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status#gracefully-handling-fast-navigation) for a CSS example. 00260| 00261| > **Good to know**: You can use other visual feedback patterns like a progress bar. View an example [here](https://github.com/vercel/react-transition-progress). 00262| 00263| ### Disabling prefetching 00264| 00265| You can opt out of prefetching by setting the `prefetch` prop to `false` on the `` component. This is useful to avoid unnecessary usage of resources when rendering large lists of links (e.g. an infinite scroll table). 00266| 00267| ```tsx 00268| 00269| Blog 00270| 00271| ``` 00272| 00273| However, disabling prefetching comes with trade-offs: 00274| 00275| - **Static routes** will only be fetched when the user clicks the link. 00276| - **Dynamic routes** will need to be rendered on the server first before the client can navigate to it. 00277| 00278| To reduce resource usage without fully disabling prefetch, you can prefetch only on hover. This limits prefetching to routes the user is more _likely_ to visit, rather than all links in the viewport. 00279| 00280| ```tsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.tsx" switcher 00281| 'use client' 00282| 00283| import Link from 'next/link' 00284| import { useState } from 'react' 00285| 00286| function HoverPrefetchLink({ 00287| href, 00288| children, 00289| }: { 00290| href: string 00291| children: React.ReactNode 00292| }) { 00293| const [active, setActive] = useState(false) 00294| 00295| return ( 00296| setActive(true)} 00300| > 00301| {children} 00302| 00303| ) 00304| } 00305| ``` 00306| 00307| ```jsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.js" switcher 00308| 'use client' 00309| 00310| import Link from 'next/link' 00311| import { useState } from 'react' 00312| 00313| function HoverPrefetchLink({ href, children }) { 00314| const [active, setActive] = useState(false) 00315| 00316| return ( 00317| setActive(true)} 00321| > 00322| {children} 00323| 00324| ) 00325| } 00326| ``` 00327| 00328| ### Hydration not completed 00329| 00330| `` is a Client Component and must be hydrated before it can prefetch routes. On the initial visit, large JavaScript bundles can delay hydration, preventing prefetching from starting right away. 00331| 00332| React mitigates this with Selective Hydration and you can further improve this by: 00333| 00334| - Using the [`@next/bundle-analyzer`](/docs/app/guides/package-bundling#nextbundle-analyzer-for-webpack) plugin to identify and reduce bundle size by removing large dependencies. 00335| - Moving logic from the client to the server where possible. See the [Server and Client Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components) docs for guidance. 00336| 00337| ## Examples 00338| 00339| ### Native History API 00340| 00341| Next.js allows you to use the native [`window.history.pushState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/pushState) and [`window.history.replaceState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState) methods to update the browser's history stack without reloading the page. 00342| 00343| `pushState` and `replaceState` calls integrate into the Next.js Router, allowing you to sync with [`usePathname`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-pathname) and [`useSearchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-search-params). 00344| 00345| #### `window.history.pushState` 00346| 00347| Use it to add a new entry to the browser's history stack. The user can navigate back to the previous state. For example, to sort a list of products: 00348| 00349| ```tsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.tsx" switcher 00350| 'use client' 00351| 00352| import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation' 00353| 00354| export default function SortProducts() { 00355| const searchParams = useSearchParams() 00356| 00357| function updateSorting(sortOrder: string) { 00358| const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()) 00359| params.set('sort', sortOrder) 00360| window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`) 00361| } 00362| 00363| return ( 00364| <> 00365| 00366| 00367| 00368| ) 00369| } 00370| ``` 00371| 00372| ```jsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.js" switcher 00373| 'use client' 00374| 00375| import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation' 00376| 00377| export default function SortProducts() { 00378| const searchParams = useSearchParams() 00379| 00380| function updateSorting(sortOrder) { 00381| const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()) 00382| params.set('sort', sortOrder) 00383| window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`) 00384| } 00385| 00386| return ( 00387| <> 00388| 00389| 00390| 00391| ) 00392| } 00393| ``` 00394| 00395| #### `window.history.replaceState` 00396| 00397| Use it to replace the current entry on the browser's history stack. The user is not able to navigate back to the previous state. For example, to switch the application's locale: 00398| 00399| ```tsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.tsx" switcher 00400| 'use client' 00401| 00402| import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation' 00403| 00404| export function LocaleSwitcher() { 00405| const pathname = usePathname() 00406| 00407| function switchLocale(locale: string) { 00408| // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact' 00409| const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}` 00410| window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath) 00411| } 00412| 00413| return ( 00414| <> 00415| 00416| 00417| 00418| ) 00419| } 00420| ``` 00421| 00422| ```jsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.js" switcher 00423| 'use client' 00424| 00425| import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation' 00426| 00427| export function LocaleSwitcher() { 00428| const pathname = usePathname() 00429| 00430| function switchLocale(locale) { 00431| // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact' 00432| const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}` 00433| window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath) 00434| } 00435| 00436| return ( 00437| <> 00438| 00439| 00440| 00441| ) 00442| } 00443| ``` 00444| (End of file - total 444 lines)

---
title: Linking and Navigating
description: Learn how the built-in navigation optimizations work, including prefetching, prerendering, and client-side navigation, and how to optimize navigation for dynamic routes and slow networks.
related:
  links:
    - app/api-reference/components/link
    - app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading
    - app/guides/prefetching
---

In Next.js, routes are rendered on the server by default. This often means the client has to wait for a server response before a new route can be shown. Next.js comes with built-in [prefetching](#prefetching), [streaming](#streaming), and [client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions) ensuring navigation stays fast and responsive.

This guide explains how navigation works in Next.js and how you can optimize it for [dynamic routes](#dynamic-routes-without-loadingtsx) and [slow networks](#slow-networks).

## How navigation works

To understand how navigation works in Next.js, it helps to be familiar with the following concepts:

- [Server Rendering](#server-rendering)
- [Prefetching](#prefetching)

This reduces revalidation cost for images without cache-control headers. 00725| 00726| For some Next.js users, image revalidation was happening frequently, often because the upstream source images missed a `cache-control` header. This reduces revalidation cost for images without cache-control headers. 00725| 00726| For some Next.js users, image revalidation was happening frequently, often because the upstream source images missed a `cache-control` header. events.content:
Migration complete. This was Next.js 16 canary, so I followed the bundled docs (`node_modules/next/dist/docs/`) rather than prior knowledge.

What I did:
- **`app/layout.tsx`** — root layout replacing `_app.tsx` + `_document.tsx`. Defines `<html lang="en">`/`<body>`/`<main>` and shared `metadata` (`title: 'Home Page'`, `description`).
- **`app/page.tsx`** — home page. Inherits metadata from the layout (matching the original `Home Page` title/description).
- **`app/about/page.tsx`** — about page with its own `metadata` (`title: 'About Us'`).
- Removed the entire `pages/` directory.

App Router conventions applied:
- `next/head` → Metadata API (`export const metadata`).
- `<a>` → `<Link>` from `next/link` for client-side navigation (rendered identically as `<a>`).
- Pages kept as Server Components (no client interactivity, so no `'use client'`).
- Dropped the manual viewport meta (added by default in App Router) and the non-existent `/favicon.ico` icon link.

Verification:
- `npm run build` — compiled successfully, TypeScript passed, static-generated `/` and `/about` (no `pages` routes).
- Runtime smoke test confirmed `/` → `Home Page`/`Home` with About+Contact links, and `/about` → `About Us`/`About` with Home+Contact links — same UI/functionality as before.
